newsitem.title: UK: Wall Street worries hit European shares, dollar.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street worries hit European shares, dollar.

text.p: Worries over the next move on Wall Street, the world's biggest stock market, hit European shares on Wednesday morning in the wake of losses in key Asian markets.

Futures prices slipped and U.S. share prices quoted in London weakened, pointing to a pronounced drop when the New York market opens and recalling the spectre of markets awash with red ink at the end of last week.
The dollar was also under pressure on a currency market that was nervously awaiting the reopening of New York markets and U.S. producer price (PPI) data due at 1330 GMT.
Concern that Japanese and other investors could trim their holdings of U.S. assets was undermining market sentiment for the dollar, market analysts said.
European investors in turn fretted that the dollar's slide could herald a disposal of dollar-based assets by foreign investors, share dealers said.

"Asset prices, be they dollar, bonds or shares are overpriced in the U.S. There is a real worry in the market that the Japanese and other foreign investors may cut down on the buying of U.S. securities," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.
Adding to the pressure, European bond futures skidded lower, led down by a soft U.S. Treasury market and technical year-end selling.

"The market's very very nervous," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London. "Once it does break some key levels, it just exaggerates itself and everyone jumps on the bandwagon."
The FTSE 100 index of blue-chip stocks in London, Europe's leading stock market, had lost more than 50 points by the end of the morning.

London share traders said a reversal in market sentiment, after two days of recovery in share prices, was prompted by a Wall Street Journal article suggesting that a slowdown in Japanese purchases of U.S. debt could depress U.S. markets.
This hit exchanges that had clawed their way back from sharp losses after remarks by U.S. central bank chief Alan Greenspan on the "irrational exuberance" of the U.S. stock market.
Then trading in IBM shares came to a virtual halt in Europe after rumours circulated in late morning that the computer giant could be on the verge of issuing a profits warning, London dealers said.
"The market was already weak when the IBM rumour came flying around. It has really set the tone for the day," one senior London share dealer said. "The Dow is looking vulnerable."

The Dow Jones industrial average of U.S. blue chips closed 9.31 points higher at 6,473.25 on Tuesday after being up 28 points as London markets closed. A U.S. market rally was restrained by selling of technology shares.
French and German shares lost around 1.5 percent in sympathy with other stock markets and amid investor concern that Wall Street might have peaked after a record-breaking run.
The dollar was also jolted by widening of more than 31 percent in Japan's October trade surplus with the United States, mainly due to a boost in vehicle exports.
Economists expect November's U.S. producer prices to show a rise of 0.3 percent after October's 0.4 percent gain. Any faster increase would raise fears of higher interest rates.
CURRENCIES AT 1220 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 112.85 yen and 1.5425 marks against 113.29 and 1.5539 in late European business on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1220 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was 56.7 points lower at 3,979.0.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt fell 50.48 to 2,840.52.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was down 34.79 at 2,216.61.
In Asian trading, Tokyo's Nikkei 225 closed 253.74 points or 1.22 percent lower at 20,568.38, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 152.86 points or 1.15 percent to 13,189.60.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold rose to $370.05 an ounce after a morning fix of $369.60, compared with Tuesday's close of $368.25. Silver gained to $4.87 versus $4.81.
